Subject: Boston Globe: Ex-Stoughton police supervisor contacted Sandra Birchmore on the day she died

Boston Globe: Ex-Stoughton police supervisor contacted Sandra Birchmore on the day she died
The former Stoughton deputy police chief retired from the force in 2022 during an internal investigation over his
interactions with Birchmore.
By Laura Crimaldi
September 15th, 2025, 6:07 AM
Secret disciplinary proceedings for a former Stoughton police deputy chief accused of sexual misconduct involving
Sandra Birchmore have revealed new details about the last day of her life and unearthed a department controversy that
had previously stayed out of public view.
The revelations were aired in June during a closed-door adjudicatory hearing conducted by the Peace Officers
Standards and Training Commission, or POST, which is seeking to sanction Robert C. Devine.
A pregnant Birchmore, 23, a former participant in a Stoughton police youth program, was found dead in her Canton
apartment on Feb. 4, 2021. Federal prosecutors last year charged former Stoughton police detective Matthew Farwell,
39, with her death. He met Birchmore through the youth program, which Devine oversaw.
The POST allegations against Devine include accusations that he had a “sexual encounter” with Birchmore while he
was on duty in December 2020 and falsely claimed that he didn’t exchange electronic messages with her.
Devine, 53, is defending himself by claiming Birchmore spread false information about him and accusing investigators of
bias. The hearing officer, Kenneth J. Fishman, a retired Superior Court judge, heard testimony in June and July, but has
yet to render a decision. The Globe obtained redacted recordings of the June proceedings.
The commission’s Division of Police Standards wants to ban Devine, who is now a lawyer, from working in law
enforcement, citing a “pattern of untruthfulness, abuse of power, and unprofessional conduct.”
Attorney Shaun Martinez, who represents the commission, revealed during his opening statement that federal
prosecutors allege Devine contacted Birchmore on Feb. 1, 2021, the day Farwell allegedly strangled her during an
evening visit to her apartment.
No other details about the communication were included in the redacted recordings.
Attorney Robert Stowe, who represents Devine, said during the hearing that the case against his client is a “big lie.”
State authorities initially ruled Birchmore killed herself. Federal prosecutors allege Farwell killed Birchmore to cover up a
sexual relationship they had been having that began when she was a minor. He has pleaded not guilty and is the only
person to face criminal charges. A pretrial conference is scheduled for next month.
Birchmore met Farwell and his twin brother, William, through the Stoughton police Explorers program, which she joined
at age 12. The Farwells had also participated in the program under Devine’s leadership when they were teenagers, and
Devine later enlisted them as volunteer instructors.
A lawsuit brought by Birchmore’s estate alleges Devine and William Farwell had sexual contact with her when she was
an adult.
Devine denies the accusations. He retired from the Stoughton force in 2022 during an internal investigation into his
interactions with Birchmore, and is no longer certified to work in law enforcement.
Investigators assumed Sandra Birchmore took her own life. What did they miss?
“The investigating officer is trying to present a lie that has been perpetrated by [Birchmore] at the behest or the
encouragement of William Farwell,” Stowe said during the June 5 hearing. “The lie is there. It’s glaring, but nobody’s
seen it.”
Stowe didn’t elaborate on that assertion in footage included in the redacted recordings. Attorney Steven Marullo, who
represents Birchmore’s estate, said the claim doesn’t make sense and hasn’t been raised in the civil case.
William Farwell entered into an agreement last September with the commission to relinquish his law enforcement
certification.
The agency had alleged he exchanged “sexually graphic text messages” and videos with Birchmore between April and
December of 2020, records show. He didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Stoughton Police Chief Donna McNamara and her former deputy, Brian Holmes, were the only witnesses to testify
during Devine’s proceedings in June. Holmes, who is now the police chief in Kingston, led a Stoughton police internal
affairs investigation concerning Birchmore.
The investigation found that Devine used the alias Marty Riggs, a character in the “Lethal Weapon” franchise, to
communicate with Birchmore on Facebook, which he disputes. As part of his defense, Devine provided internal
investigators with documentation showing he’s been targeted by hackers, Stowe said.
During the hearing, Stowe questioned Holmes and McNamara about their relationships with Devine. Stowe also
inquired about an incident during which Holmes retrieved a note written in crayon from his department mailbox, which
read, “Revenge is a meal best served cold.”
The testimony linked the note to a 2016 visit to the police station by Devine’s 8-year-old daughter, who was using
crayons.
The girl’s visit occurred soon after Devine had returned to duty following his demotion from deputy chief to patrol officer
and a 60-day unpaid suspension. The sanctions were triggered by an internal affairs investigation, which found Devine
directed a subordinate to look into harassing messages he was receiving as he attempted to end an extramarital affair.
In that case, Devine also claimed he was targeted by hackers.
McNamara testified she directed a lieutenant to investigate the note.
“Do you recall that his 8-year-old daughter was given a trespass notice, saying that she couldn’t come near the police
station?” Stowe asked McNamara.
She said that the girl “wasn’t allowed in the station without my authorization.”
During Holmes’s testimony, he said he and Devine had been friends earlier in their careers, but he distanced himself
from Devine in about 2011. He gave several reasons for his decision, including concerns that Devine’s interactions with
an adult who previously participated in the Explorers program were “getting way too cozy.”
The former explorer was not Birchmore, Holmes said, though his response to a question about the timing of Devine’s
interactions with the former explorer was redacted.
Holmes testified that he wasn’t biased against Devine, but anticipated that Devine would make that allegation and
recused himself from interviewing him during the internal affairs probe.
Also, according to testimony, an examination of Birchmore’s electronic communications revealed Devine’s reaction to
her raising the possibility that Matthew Farwell had fathered her unborn child.
“The response was something along the lines of, ‘You shouldn’t be talking to me about this. You shouldn’t be talking to
anybody about this,’” Holmes testified.
DNA testing has excluded Matthew Farwell as the father of Birchmore’s unborn baby, and it’s unclear if authorities have
made a determination about paternity.
POST was established in 2020 amid a state police reform effort that followed the killing of George Floyd by a police
officer in Minneapolis. It certifies officers, investigates misconduct, and sets training standards. Law enforcement
officers in Massachusetts must be certified by the commission to work.
Fishman, the hearing officer, closed the proceedings, but later authorized the release of recordings. The Globe obtained
redacted recordings of the June proceedings from attorney Howard Friedman, a civil rights lawyer who got them through
a public records request. The Globe requested a copy in July, but the commission has yet to provide them.
